doc.title: Jackie Cain and Roy Kral interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998

chapter: Cello group, family and the road
title: Culture loss, jazz education and learning by doing
summary: Traditional cultures fading, jazz programs in colleges, the need to play in front of audiences, and Japanese players lacking swing.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Yeah. Well just like all the traditional things from different parts of the world, you know, as far as dress goes or customs, I mean it’s all getting lost. I mean even in India they don’t make the beautiful cloth and fabric that they used to make. I mean they invented paisley and all these beautiful things and now they’re wearing, you see guys with baseball hats and jeans. The young people are into that, which is kind of sad. It’s just like losing the culture of the American Indians. How many people make rugs, Indian rugs, anymore? It’s a dying art. And music is the same. But some people try and keep it alive.

However, I believe that this music we’re involved with will live forever, and eventually there’ll be a huge resurgence of interest in it. Because everyone is eventually going to get tired of loud and too basic. We notice that already.

Well as they say, from your voice to God’s ears. You know they say that because it would be nice if more people — but you know with all the college programs and things that are happening concerning learning jazz and studying it and everything, I think that’s going to help it a lot. Although you know in the old days you learned on your own by going out and doing it. And that’s really key also. Once you know something about it and you’re good at it, you have to get out there and practice it in front of an audience and develop your own style and so forth.
Let me see there’s North Texas State, which is kind of wonderful, Berklee, and —
William Paterson, near us, excellent. And you guys up there at your school.

There’s Eastman School of Music also. There’s lots of — but so many people say that, veteran musicians, that you have to get out there and do it and play with lots of different people and I suppose someday someone may be able to come up with a program where you’re in college but you do a semester out in the clubs somehow.

Well you’d have to be a good player to get into the clubs and be allowed to sit in, because there’s so many good players now that it’s unbelievable. It’s wonderful. So there is a great future for this music.

Just like when you go to Japan you know, you hear players over there that are fantastic, they’re just ridiculous. But there’s one thing missing sometimes, and that’s a certain swing and a certain feeling that they don’t get. It sounds very — how can I express it — it’s just mechanical in a way. But I mean their technique just overwhelms you. My God they’re so wonderful. But there’s sometimes little things missing.
In jazz. That’s what I meant, right.
